name: Old Kanembu / Tarjumo, 'the language of the glosses
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Bondarev, Dmitry. 2006. The language of the glosses in the Bornu quranic manuscripts. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 69(1): 113-140. catalog_locator: BSOAS 2006 p.123 (section III 'The language of the glosses: morphology and phonology', with fn.8) and p.129 (tone marking / weak letters); Bondarev & Dobronravin 2019 pp.249 and 252; Bondarev 2005 draft p.4
catalog_quote: [p.123] LG represents an older form of Kanuri. A brief note on some linguistic features of Kanuri will therefore prove useful before LG is described. ... Their deciphering might be complicated by the fact that Kanuri is a tonal language, with three distinctive tones: high, low and falling.8 [fn.8] The high tone is indicated here with an acute accent (e.g. á), the low tone is unmarked (a), the falling tone is marked by circumflex (â). [p.129] The second problem is connected to tone marking. The question whether the Bornu writing system distinguishes tones is still open. If it does so, then to what extent? Does it work on a regular basis, or is it optional? ... These examples show that the long syllables (in graphic form) of the morphemes of the LG correspond to the modern Kanuri high tone syllables in these respective morphemes. ... In other words, which particular feature do the weak letters represent: high tone, long vowels, or both?
world_status: statement found in an open source

The question whethe…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Old Kanembu (the language of the Qur'anic glosses, ancestor of modern Tarjumo) is analysed as an archaic variety of Kanuri, a three-tone language (H, L, Falling); the Arabic-script 'weak letters' appear to encode high (and falling) tone. No statement locates word stress; the companion paper (Bondarev 2005/2007, Afrika und Uebersee 88, draft p.4) explicitly leaves open whether the script marks 'tones? length? stress? a combination'.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author flags that tone marking in the script may be optional/irregular and that a long/short vowel contrast in LG is not supported by the evidence.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the tonal system of Kanuri as inherited by written Old Kanembu and what the manuscript orthography encodes; no description of stress in citation forms or of the prosody of modern Tarjumo recitation was found in the open sources.
new_statements.identity_note: The sources describe 'Old Kanembu' = 'the language of the glosses (LG)' in 16th-18th c. Borno Qur'an manuscripts and its modern liturgical descendant Tarjumo, used by Kanuri scholars for Qur'anic exegesis; Glottolog subsumes both under tarj1235 (ISO txj). It is a learned written/recited register with no native speakers, analysed by Bondarev as an archaic variety of Kanuri; the tonal characterisation (H/L/F) is stated for Kanuri (kanu1279 / Central Kanuri cent2050) and carried over to LG, whose script appears to encode high/falling tone. No first-hand description of the prosody of spoken/recited Tarjumo was found.

new_statements.quote: [p.252] ...while others are more region-specific and only shared within a literacy contact area (like the letter kāf for k and ghain for g, or the Arabic "weak" letters used for suprasegmental features such as the combination of stress and tone); ... Some high frequency items in Old Kanembu could also have been encoded in a more standardised way due to their prosodic prominence at the end of an intonational phrase, as is evidenced in modern day practices of commenting the Qur'an in Tarjumo. Many phrase-final and sentence-final items (e.g. [ʧígí:] 'there is', [gȅn:] 'in') have such a prominent pitch and length in Tarjumo recitations that the whole practice of commenting the Qur'an is sometimes referred to by laymen as 'cigi and gen recitation'. [p.249] ...the use of hāʾ could have been motivated by phonological features such as high tone or length of the vowel

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (334-page OAPEN volume, text present; chapter = pp.246-278 = print pp.237-269). extracted text of p.262 (print p.252, sec. 3.4 'General tendencies in Kanuri orthography') carries the quoted passage verbatim: '..while others are more region-specific and only shared within a literacy contact area (like the letter kaf for k and ghain for g, or the Arabic "weak" letters used for suprasegmental features such as the combination of stress and tone)..' and 'Some high frequency items in Old Kanembu could also have been encoded in a more standardised way due to their prosodic prominence at the end of an intonational phrase, as is evidenced in modern day practices of commenting the Qur'an in Ta…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Bondarev 2006 statement (tone language, no stress statement): the work again treats the language as tonal (high tone vs length as the candidate features behind the weak-letter spellings) and adds two details: (a) the Arabic weak letters in this literacy area are said to encode 'the combination of stress and tone', i.e. the authors assume some stress exists alongside tone, but without locating it; (b) phrase-/sentence-final items in Tarjumo recitation carry prominent pitch and length ('cigi and gen recitation'). Section 4 (pp.253-269) is about Hausa Ajami (Chadic), not this language.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The chapter treats Old Kanembu/Tarjumo (and Kanuri) as a tone language: it discusses whether the Arabic weak letters and final ha' encode high tone or vowel length, reads imala+alif as 'either prosodic long [e:] or a high tone /e/', and says the weak letters in this literacy area encode 'suprasegmental features such as the combination of stress and tone'. It never says where word stress falls or whether it is contrastive; the only prominence it locates is phrase-level: phrase-final and sentence-final items carry prominent pitch and length in Tarjumo recitation.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. The orthographic discussion notes that final /o/ words and function words behave differently for the final ha' convention, but that is orthography, not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The chapter's Kanuri sections (3.1-3.4, pp.240-252) describe Old Kanembu/Tarjumo as attested in Borno Qur'anic manuscripts (MS.3ImI dated 1669, MS.2ShK, MS.Konduga, MS.1YM, MS.Arabe 402), in late-19th-century Kanuri gargam manuscripts, and in modern Tarjumo recitation practice of Kanuri scholars; the phrase-final prominence remark is about present-day Tarjumo recitations. Section 4 (pp.253-269) describes Hausa Ajami, a different language (Chadic), and is not about tarj1235.

For completeness I a full-text search for stress/accent the other on-disk Old Kanembu texts in the same directory (not listed works, not added): Bondarev 2005 draft p.4 asks 'which particular suprasegmental feature is marked in LG: tones? length? stress? a combination of tone and other features?' (an open question, no placement statement), and the 2006 BSOAS, 2006 JQS, 2010, 2020, 2022 texts mention only tone marking with acute accents; none states word-stress placement. Nothing missed.

tone.quote: it is difficult to be sure which particular suprasegmental feature is marked in LG: tones? length? stress? a combination of tone and other features? ... This form may represent the LG imperfective -ì (low tone) paradigm ... Given the current state of research it is impossible, however, to arrive at a definitive conclusion about the suprasegmental features of the perfective-imperfective distinction in LG. It might be parallel to the Kanuri/Kanembu high-low opposition (high -í = PRF, low -ì = IMPF), but other possibilities (like the complex correlation in Beria) cannot be ruled out either.
